extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv teachers, and sketch comedy performers/coaches
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative criteria for performing, coaching, and writing improvised and sketch comedy scenes; includes exercises, diagnosis of common performer problems, and rules for audience-feedback games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightening / Raising the stakes / Accelerating the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene should accelerate: characters become more agitated/blatant, stakes increase, and the absurdity can climb (also called 'heightening' or 'going up the absurdity curve').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a calm platform to give the scene somewhere to go. Increase agitation or bluntness across beats (doctor/patient example). Use heightening deliberately to build momentum and create escalation toward a point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern setup and repetition as a sketch mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketches often operate by setting up a pattern and repeating it, providing a template into which jokes can be fitted (e.g., Constable Savage sketch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the pattern escalate in bizarreness and raise stakes. Arrange repeated beats so each iteration adds something. Recognize that improvisation may struggle to generate the perfectly ordered acceleration patterns that written sketch comedy can.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding the Game (identifying the scene's structural 'game')
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'game' is the structural pattern that gives a scene its comedic engine; in some scenes the game is the scene's structure rather than incidental behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If finding-the-game is the goal, accept that the game becomes the structure; but be cautious—relying solely on quick game-finding (e.g., in three lines) limits scope and may strip human feeling from the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with a platform (establishing the world)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a calm, clear platform that defines the world and normality, so there is 'somewhere to go' in the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The platform helps the audience recognise what's extraordinary. Provide specific, observable details so reincorporation and narrative change become possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaking routines as a storytelling device
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaking established routines provides 'point' and can serve narrative purpose—this is a key Johnstone technique for moving an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use breaking routines to supply emotional or narrative impact; recognize it is often the opposite of finding-the-game and can be difficult to combine with pattern-focused approaches, though both are valid tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reincorporation, canceling, or completing routines to end a scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Use reincorporation, cancellation, or completion of patterns to provide closure and end scenes effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan or notice how earlier elements can be brought back or resolved to create satisfying endings rather than relying on arbitrary stopping points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage transitions between pattern segments and narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: When repetition becomes the point, transitions between the pattern and the rest of the story must be carefully managed to avoid frustrating the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider light overlapping patterns if needed, but remember in find-the-game scenes the game is the structure; ensure the audience can follow the shift from pattern to story and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make early promises to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience wants to see a 'point'—they will continue watching if they believe something good is coming based on early promises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the first minute, create an enticing promise (a narrative question or situation). Deliver on that promise within the next beat; then make another promise to sustain interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continue or Thank You (audience feedback game rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise/game to test whether scenes have promise: perform for sixty seconds, freeze and ask the group 'Continue or thank you?'; if majority says Continue, proceed and freeze every thirty seconds thereafter until 'Thank you'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell improvisers most won't get a Continue first time to lower expectations. After a Thank you, ask the group why to provide concrete feedback. Majority rules; use freezes as learning moments to analyse promise/delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliver on promises then make another promise
rubrics_metrics.description: Any promise will do, but you must deliver on it; once delivered, create a new promise to keep the audience engaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If performers waffle or 'bridge' instead of fulfilling the promise, the audience will lose faith and say 'Thank you'. Even small promises (e.g., 'I have something to tell you') can secure a Continue if followed up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor audience suggestions (meet implied expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the audience supplies a suggestion (e.g., 'Casino'), that suggestion implies a set of expectations; performers should aim to deliver the sort of scenario the suggester hopes to see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating a suggestion literally in a way that deflates implied stakes (e.g., making 'Casino' a scene about failing to get change). Think about genre and stakes audiences expect from that prompt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest, specific group feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: After exercises like Continue or Thank You, it's crucial to ask why the group chose 'Thank you' or 'Continue' so performers learn specific reasons for audience responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage constructive specificity ('You promised to show the cellar, then you talked instead') rather than vague negativity. If performers don't ask, they squander the learning opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use group problem-solving mentality (remove ego)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach rehearsal exercises as collaborative problems to solve (a 'group Sudoku'), so performers focus on solving the scene rather than taking failures personally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage shared responsibility, celebrate small wins (getting one 'Continue'), and foster an atmosphere where performers experiment without ego-driven fear of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seen Enough game (audience-leaves variant) as a teaching tool
rubrics_metrics.description: In Seen Enough, audience members leave when they've seen enough; surviving longer is a measure of engagement and teaches performers to make strong offers quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keith Johnstone suggests lasting even seven seconds is an achievement; use the game to build fearlessness and to learn what audience-read cues turn them off quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a good state (positivity, relaxation, readiness to risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisers should be in a relaxed, happy state to take risks and tell spontaneous stories; this state makes process easier and results more engaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on exercises that move students out of anxieties. A good state enables players to accept obvious ideas, support partners, and attempt bold choices without crippling fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extremes: neither facile gags nor indulgent worthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Too-facile, glib, anything-for-a-laugh work is unsatisfying; conversely, overly worthy, introspective work that lacks structure bores the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't pander (e.g., opening with lowbrow jokes that set narrow expectations). Balance comedy and narrative; build scope early so audiences understand the show's tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvisation as storytelling (define hero, world, and normality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisation inherently tells stories: identify who the hero is, what the world looks like, and what counts as normal so the extraordinary is recognisable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on A affecting B and on breaking routines to cause change. Use reincorporation and obvious details to anchor the world, and accept that surprise is a rare commodity in stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core vs superficial skills: prioritise storytelling and good state
rubrics_metrics.description: Core skills (being in a good state, storytelling, breaking routines, reacting) matter more than superficial tricks (physicality, rhymes, parodies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop core skills first; superficial devices can dazzle but without core work the material will feel cold or glib. Emphasise warmth and human feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continued training balance: coach, peer work, and stage time
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective ongoing training combines coached work, rehearsing with peers at your level, and actual performances in front of audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-dependence on coaches (intimidation) and avoid only self-teaching (reinventing the wheel). Use a mix to develop independence while receiving feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting and company composition responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: When casting a company, directors/coaches have the right to choose who stays in the company; you are not obliged to work with people who don't fit or who impede the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to get the best from people you work with, but be prepared to say goodbye if it's not working; invest in people whose core qualities make it worthwhile to address their weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnosis principle: most problems stem from fear or ego
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost all improviser problems reduce to fear or ego issues; keep this in mind when diagnosing and prescribing corrective exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor interventions to whether the root cause is reluctance, over-performance, people-pleasing, or other ego/fear manifestations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem rubric — 'Wimps' (symptoms, diagnosis, cure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wimps: reluctant to enter scenes, reluctant to commit, play slowly, wait for others to lead, may produce a brilliant opening then freeze.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis: lack conviction in ideas and over-cautiousness. Cure: place performer in safe supportive atmosphere and push with exercises demanding speed and spontaneity (Standing Wave, New Choice, Over-confessing, Master/Servant Dubbing). Do not cosset; make them try and show they can.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem rubric — 'Joker' (symptoms, diagnosis, cure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokers compulsively try to be funny, editorialise rather than emote, force absurdity, or steer to taboo topics; may be charming but can derail stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis: belief that it's their responsibility to make things funny or fear of emotional material. Cure: teacher enforces zero tolerance for unnecessary gagging; give scenes where success comes from commitment and emotional truth (example: shy teenagers scene); use observation-focused games (e.g., It's Tuesday) to build reactive skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem rubric — 'Yes Man' (symptoms, diagnosis, cure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes Men accept every idea blindly, avoid unpleasant characters, solve problems too neatly, and prevent story middles from developing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis: comfortable with acceptance but uncomfortable with dramatic tension; people-pleasing personality. Cure: use feedback games (The King Game, 'Nope!', The Removalists) to encourage making dramatic offers and sometimes failing to solve problems so middles can take off.
